---
title: "Analysis 1: How well do computational methods predict experimental ΔΔG?"
author: "Luis Sebastian Galán, Laura Grenaa Jensen, Taniya Dey and Thota Kanishka Rao"
format: html
---

## Setup

```{r}
library("tidyverse")
library("here")
library("broom")
```

## Load data

We load the augmented dataset and keep only variants that have a
prediction from all six computational methods, so every method is
compared on the same variants.

```{r}
dat_aug <- read_csv(here("data", "03_dat_aug.csv"))

dat_pred <- dat_aug |>
  drop_na(ends_with("_ddg")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = ends_with("_ddg"),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "predicted_ddg"
  ) |>
  mutate(method = str_remove(method, "_ddg"))

dat_pred |>
  count(method)
```

## Predicted vs. experimental ΔΔG

Each point is one mutation. If a method predicted perfectly, all points
would lie on a straight line. The blue line is a linear fit.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
dat_pred |>
  ggplot(aes(x = predicted_ddg, y = ddg)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x) +
  facet_wrap(~ method, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    x = "Predicted ΔΔG",
    y = "Experimental ΔΔG (kcal/mol)",
    title = "Predicted vs. experimental ΔΔG for each computational method"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## One linear model per method

We fit one linear model per method, `ddg ~ predicted_ddg`, using
`nest()` and `map()`. From each model we take the R squared (how much of
the variation in experimental ΔΔG the method explains) and the slope with
its p-value. We also compute the Spearman correlation, which is less
sensitive to the extreme values that some methods produce.

```{r}
models <- dat_pred |>
  group_by(method) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model = map(data, ~ lm(ddg ~ predicted_ddg, data = .x)),
    glance = map(model, glance),
    tidy = map(model, tidy),
    spearman = map_dbl(
      data,
      ~ cor(.x$ddg, .x$predicted_ddg, method = "spearman")
    )
  )

model_summary <- models |>
  unnest(glance) |>
  select(method, r_squared = r.squared, spearman) |>
  left_join(
    models |>
      unnest(tidy) |>
      filter(term == "predicted_ddg") |>
      select(method, slope = estimate, p_value = p.value),
    by = "method"
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(desc(r_squared))

model_summary
```

## Comparing the methods

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
model_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = r_squared, y = fct_reorder(method, r_squared))) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(r_squared, 2)), hjust = -0.2) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    x = "R squared (variation in experimental ΔΔG explained)",
    y = NULL,
    title = "How well each method predicts experimental ΔΔG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Conclusion

All six methods have a positive and significant slope, so higher
predicted ΔΔG goes with higher experimental ΔΔG. But every method explains
less than 8% of the variation in experimental ΔΔG (R squared below 0.08).
FoldX and Discovery Studio (d_studio) predict best, with the highest
R squared and Spearman correlation. The statistical potentials (dfire,
ddfire) explain the least.

Note that many experimental ΔΔG values sit at exactly 8 kcal/mol. These
look like a cap used for mutations where binding was lost completely,
which limits how well any method can fit them.
